## Relation to CFA Trees 

The SEM-tree analyses used in the present study are closely related to CFA trees [@Goretzko2026] and represent a particular specification of the broader SEM-tree framework rather than a distinct method. 
Both embed a prespecified confirmatory factor model within model-based recursive partitioning. 
In the present study, metric and scalar MNI were investigated using score-based instability tests focused on factor loadings and item intercepts, respectively, while other free parameters were not globally fixed across the tree. 
By contrast, the intercept-focused CFA-tree approach described by @Goretzko2026 fix nonfocal parameters to estimates from a single-group CFA, thereby more explicitly isolating intercept instability tests. 

This distinction is relevant to the present findings. 
Despite focusing the metric instability test on loadings, intercept-only MNI produced elevated metric rejection rates in several conditions. 
Thus, restricting the focal parameters did not ensure that the test responded exclusively to loading heterogeneity. 
More strongly constraining nonfocal parameters, as in the CFA-tree approach, might improve parameter-level attribution, although the present simulation did not examine whether this would reduce cross-level sensitivity or introduce other forms of misspecification. 

A potential direction for future research could be to investigate a sequential MI procedure in which parameter constraints are progressively relaxed. 
Rather than beginning with a loading-focused SEM tree in which nonfocal parameters remain freely estimated, metric invariance could initially be evaluated using a more strongly constrained CFA-tree specification, as described by @Goretzko2026. 
By fixing nonfocal parameters, this approach would aim to isolate loading instability and reduce the possibility that heterogeneity in other model parameters influences the metric test. 
If metric invariance is retained, subsequent scalar testing could relax selected constraints while evaluating instability in item intercepts. 
Such a strategy would reverse the popular constraint structure examined in the present study, moving from a more restricted metric analysis toward a more flexible scalar analysis. 
Whether stronger constraints improve the localization of MNI however remains to be seen. 
The present findings demonstrate that cross-level sensitivity can arise even when nonfocal parameters remain freely estimated, indicating that parameter-focused instability tests do not necessarily isolate heterogeneity in the corresponding parameter class. 
Conversely, fixing nonfocal parameters may introduce misspecification when those parameters are genuinely noninvariant, potentially producing similar cross-level effects. 
Thus, neither strategy guarantees that detected instability can be attributed exclusively to the focal parameters.  
An additional consideration is the identification of latent means. 
Because observed subgroup differences can arise from latent mean differences, intercept noninvariance, or both, their attribution depends on the constraints imposed on the model. 
As discussed by @Goretzko2026, fixing latent means may cause genuine differences in the latent construct to appear as intercept instability, whereas constraining intercepts while allowing latent means to vary may produce the opposite attribution. 
Consequently, stronger parameter constraints cannot automatically be assumed to yield more accurate identification of MNI. 
Future research should examine how alternative constraint and identification strategies affect both cross-level sensitivity and the distinction between measurement noninvariance and substantive latent mean differences. 

These findings also support the integration of tree-based procedures into broader MI assessment workflows rather than their use as standalone methods. 
Tree-based approaches are particularly useful when potential moderators, nonlinearities, interactions, or cutoffs are not known in advance, whereas MNLFA is advantageous when moderator effects can be theoretically specified and parameter-level estimates are of substantive interest. 
Rather than viewing these methods as competing alternatives, @Goretzko2026 recommends integrating tree-based procedures into established MI assessment workflows, such as those discussed by @Somaraju2022, alongside approaches such as MGCFA or MNLFA. 
Trees can identify previously unspecified sources and patterns of heterogeneity, which can subsequently be examined using explicitly parameterized measurement models. 
Such complementary analyses are particularly valuable given the cross-level sensitivity observed in the present study, which cautions against interpreting tree-based instability as unambiguous evidence of a specific level of MNI. 
Furthermore the exploratory PDPs in this study suggest that they could also complement a tree based approach to MI-testing by approximating the functional form of the moderation. 
However, one should try to grow a stable forest, as to not overestimate results from a computationally constrained SEM forest, like in this study. 
The resulting patterns should then be interpreted as preliminary indications of moderation patterns rather than definitive estimates of the underlying functional forms. 
 
Regularization offers a further extension to the presented approaches and can be particularly useful for complex measurement models or when many potential sources of MNI are under consideration.
Within exploratory factor analyses, regularization can be used to obtain sparse and interpretable loading structures without relying on conventional factor rotation [@Goretzko2025], whereas within MNLFA, regularization has been applied to moderation parameters to identify measurement bias across multiple categorical and continuous background characteristics [@Bauer2020; @Belzak2024]. 
Although such extensions can reduce the need to prespecify individual sources of measurement heterogeneity, they also introduce additional methodological choices concerning penalization and model selection. 
Method choice and combination should therefore be guided by the analytical objective.  

## Limitations and Future Research

Also please note, that we inspected the ninth wave of SHARE, Whereas @BonnevilleRoussy2024 investigated the waves two and seven. 
The empirical example therefore illustrates that MNLFA and SEM trees can yield broadly convergent substantive conclusions while providing different descriptions of the underlying measurement heterogeneity. 

Several limitations qualify the generalizability of the present findings. 
First, the simulation considered linear, quadratic, and sigmoidal moderation, representing distinct but not exhaustive forms of MNI. 
Although SEM trees performed comparatively consistently across these conditions, this advantage cannot be generalized to arbitrary functional relationships. 
Second, the simulation employed a relatively simple one-factor model with four continuous indicators. 
Future studies should examine whether the observed performance patterns extend to more complex measurement structures, including multifactor models, ordinal indicators, cross-loadings, and correlated residuals.

The simulation also largely separated the detection of MNI from moderator selection by supplying SEM trees with the relevant moderator variables. 
Although EFA trees have previously been evaluated in the presence of irrelevant candidate covariates (@Sterner2023), and methodological work on SEM trees has examined selection bias and multiple-testing adjustments (@Arnold2021), the additional noise-predictor analysis in the present study addressed these issues only under restricted conditions. 
Future research should therefore investigate how parameter-focused CFA-based trees perform with larger sets of correlated and irrelevant moderators, particularly regarding the probability of selecting the true source of MNI, the stability of selected variables and split points, and the trade-off between false-positive selections and statistical power. 
Such investigations are especially relevant because a selected moderator may act as a proxy for another correlated source of measurement heterogeneity.

The empirical application was intended to illustrate the methods rather than establish definitive age or cultural thresholds in the CASP-12. 
Importantly, the present study analyzed SHARE wave 9, whereas @BonnevilleRoussy2024 investigated waves 2 and 7. 
Differences between the findings may therefore reflect variation in sample composition or measurement properties across waves, as well as methodological differences. 
Although MNLFA and SEM trees yielded broadly convergent substantive conclusions in the present application, they characterized the underlying heterogeneity differently. 
Replication across SHARE waves and independent samples would help establish the stability of the identified moderators, age partitions, and item-level parameter differences.
